## Merit Systems in Government {.section-slide data-background-color="#102a43"}

## Hurricane Dorian, 2019

:::: {.columns .dorian}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](images/trump-dorian-altered-map-2019.jpg){.dorian-photo fig-alt="President Trump in the Oval Office holding a NOAA forecast map of Hurricane Dorian, with the cone of uncertainty extended into Alabama in black marker."}

[White House video, September 4, 2019 (public domain)]{.photo-credit}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Sept. 1: the President says Alabama will likely be hit "(much) harder than anticipated"
- About 20 minutes later, the NWS office in Birmingham posts that Alabama will see no impacts
- Sept. 4: the forecast map, extended into Alabama with a marker
- Sept. 6: NOAA issues an unsigned statement saying Birmingham "spoke in absolute terms"
:::
::::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
10 minutes with your table:
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Who should the Birmingham forecasters answer to: the President, NOAA leadership, the public, or the science?
- Was NOAA's statement appropriate political responsiveness, or political interference? Where is the line?
- If you were one of the forecasters, what would you do next, and what protections would you need to do it?
:::

## Politics and Government Employment

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">Political responsiveness</span>

Elected leaders set direction. Career staff carry out the policies voters chose, even ones they disagree with.

</div>
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">Neutral competence</span>

Hiring and firing turn on qualifications and performance, so staff can tell leaders what they do not want to hear.

</div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
The question is how much political responsiveness is appropriate, and who decides where to draw the line.
:::

## A Brief History of the Civil Service

::: {.timeline}
<div class="tl-step fragment"><span class="tl-year">1829–1881</span><span class="card-heading">Spoils</span><p>Jobs reward party loyalty; each election turns over offices</p></div>
<div class="tl-step fragment"><span class="tl-year">1881</span><span class="card-heading">A policy window</span><p>President Garfield is shot by a disappointed office-seeker</p></div>
<div class="tl-step fragment accent-step"><span class="tl-year">1883</span><span class="card-heading">Pendleton Act</span><p>Open competitive exams; no firing for refusing political contributions. Covers ~10% of jobs at first</p></div>
<div class="tl-step fragment"><span class="tl-year">1912 · 1939</span><span class="card-heading">Extending it</span><p>Lloyd–La Follette lets employees petition Congress. The Hatch Act limits partisan activity. Social Security amendments require merit systems in grant-funded state programs</p></div>
<div class="tl-step fragment"><span class="tl-year">1978</span><span class="card-heading">Civil Service Reform Act</span><p>OPM, MSPB, FLRA, and the Senior Executive Service</p></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Having employees is not the same as having a capable government.
:::

## The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">The problem by the 1970s</span>

Employees were hard to evaluate and harder to remove. "Turkey farms" held people no one could fire. One commission hired, set rules, *and* judged appeals.

</div>
<div class="compare-side accent"><span class="card-heading">The CSRA's answer</span>

Split the jobs up. **OPM** runs personnel policy. **MSPB** hears appeals. **FLRA** oversees labor relations. Add performance management and a mobile Senior Executive Service.

</div>
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
How can a system protect employees from political firing without also protecting poor performers? 
:::

## Merit Principles and Prohibited Personnel Practices

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">9 merit system principles</span>

Goals for how the federal workforce should be managed (5 U.S.C. § 2301).

</div>
<div class="compare-side accent"><span class="card-heading">14 prohibited personnel practices</span>

Actions that are against the law (5 U.S.C. § 2302). A manager can be disciplined for them, and employees harmed by one can seek corrective action.

</div>
:::

## The Nine Merit System Principles

```{=html}
<div class="mp-grid">
<div class="mp"><span class="mp-label">1 · Recruitment, selection, and advancement</span><p>Recruit from all segments of society; select and advance on ability, knowledge, and skills after fair and open competition</p></div>
<div class="mp"><span class="mp-label">2 · Equity</span><p>Fair and equitable treatment regardless of political affiliation, race, sex, religion, age, disability, or marital status</p></div>
<div class="mp"><span class="mp-label">3 · Compensation</span><p>Equal pay for work of equal value; incentives and recognition for excellent performance</p></div>
<div class="mp"><span class="mp-label">4 · Conduct</span><p>High standards of integrity, conduct, and concern for the public interest</p></div>
<div class="mp"><span class="mp-label">5 · Utilization</span><p>Use the workforce efficiently and effectively</p></div>
<div class="mp"><span class="mp-label">6 · Retention</span><p>Retain employees based on performance; correct poor performance, and separate those who cannot or will not improve</p></div>
<div class="mp"><span class="mp-label">7 · Training and development</span><p>Provide training where it improves individual and organizational performance</p></div>
<div class="mp"><span class="mp-label">8 · Partisan neutrality</span><p>Protect employees from favoritism, arbitrary action, and political coercion</p></div>
<div class="mp"><span class="mp-label">9 · Public interest</span><p>Protect employees who report lawbreaking, mismanagement, waste, abuse of authority, or dangers to public health and safety</p></div>
</div>
```

## The Merit in Merit Principles

- The goal is an ethical, competent, and effective workforce with high integrity that serves the public interest
- Written for the federal civil service, but good principles for all public service employment
  - State and local governments
  - Nonprofit organizations
- The principles line up with the NASPAA competencies for public service (Guy & Sowa, Table 3.3)


## Prohibited Personnel Practices

- Enumerated by the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978
- Hold both supervisors and employees accountable
- Connect how people are treated to how the organization performs:

::: {.pathway .ppp-path}
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">Inputs</span><p>The people in the organization</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">Process</span><p>How people are trained, developed, promoted, and rewarded</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">Outputs</span><p>The quantity and quality of services delivered</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">Outcomes</span><p>Results achieved for the mission</p></div>
:::

## The 14 Prohibited Personnel Practices

::: {.ppp-list}
1. Discriminate for or against an employee or applicant
2. Consider recommendations not based on personal knowledge or records
3. Coerce political activity, or retaliate for refusing it
4. Deceive or obstruct anyone's right to compete for a job
5. Influence anyone to withdraw from competition
6. Grant a preference not authorized by law
7. Hire, promote, or advocate for a relative (nepotism)
8. Retaliate against whistleblowers
9. Retaliate for filing an appeal, complaint, or grievance, cooperating with an Inspector General, or refusing to break the law
10. Discriminate based on conduct that does not affect job performance
11. Violate veterans' preference requirements
12. Violate any law, rule, or regulation implementing the merit principles
13. Enforce a nondisclosure agreement that lacks the required whistleblower-protection language
14. Access an employee's or applicant's medical records as part of any of the above
:::

::: {.lead-in}
The book lists 13. The 14th was added in 2017.
:::

## Activity: Allowed or Prohibited? {.activity-slide data-background-color="#176b87"}

```{=html}
<div class="poll-grid">
<div class="poll-item"><p>1. A division chief recommends her nephew for an opening in her own division.</p><span class="poll-answer fragment">Prohibited: nepotism</span></div>
<div class="poll-item"><p>2. A supervisor asks staff to help on a candidate's campaign. People who say no get the weekend shifts.</p><span class="poll-answer fragment">Prohibited: coerced political activity</span></div>
<div class="poll-item"><p>3. A hiring panel adds points to a veteran's score.</p><span class="poll-answer fragment">Allowed, in fact required for eligible veterans. Violating veterans' preference is the prohibited practice.</span></div>
<div class="poll-item"><p>4. A manager tells a strong outside applicant not to bother, because the job is "already spoken for."</p><span class="poll-answer fragment">Prohibited: obstructing or discouraging competition</span></div>
</div>
```


## Due Process: *Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill*

::: {.scenario}
<span class="card-heading">The case (1985)</span>

A school security guard is fired for failing to disclose a past felony conviction on his application. He gets no chance to respond before he is fired.
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
The Supreme Court held that a civil servant removable only for cause has a property interest in the job. Before firing: notice, an explanation of the evidence, and a chance to respond.
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Does the public benefit from this protection, or only the employee?
:::

## Removing Civil Service Protections: Schedule F

:::: {.columns .schedf}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**What it does**

- Creates a new category for career positions that are "confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating"
- Employees are still hired on merit, stay career (not political) appointees, and keep protection from prohibited personnel practices and whistleblower retaliation
- But they lose the adverse-action procedures and MSPB appeal rights from slide 14. Agencies can remove them with written notice.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Timeline**

- **Oct. 2020:** created as "Schedule F" (EO 13957)
- **Jan. 2021:** rescinded (EO 14003)
- **Jan. 2025:** reinstated as "Schedule Policy/Career" (EO 14171)
- **Feb. 2026:** OPM final rule
- **June 2026:** about 8,000 positions moved, 97% at GS-15 or senior level
- Union lawsuits are pending
:::
::::

::: {.source-line}
Sources: [OPM news release, Feb. 5, 2026](https://www.opm.gov/news/news-releases/opm-finalizes-schedule-policycareer-rule-to-strengthen-accountability/) · [CRS, *Schedule Policy/Career: 2026 Final Rule, Legal Challenges, and Issues for Lawmakers* (LSB11412), Mar. 26, 2026](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB11412) · [FedSmith, June 3, 2026](https://www.fedsmith.com/2026/06/03/what-the-new-schedule-policy-career-order-means-for-federal-employees/)
:::

## Schedule F: Arguments For and Against

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">For</span>

Policy-influencing career staff should answer to elected leaders. Leaders need to be able to remove staff who resist the agenda voters chose.

</div>
<div class="compare-side accent"><span class="card-heading">Against</span>

Without appeal rights, the risk Pendleton addressed returns. The staff most likely to be removed are the ones whose job is to tell leaders unwelcome facts.

</div>
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Back to Birmingham: if the forecasters could be removed with written notice, what would they have posted?
:::

## HRM in Nonprofit Organizations {.section-slide data-background-color="#102a43"}

## Nonprofits in the United States

::: {.stat-row}
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-number">~12M</span><p>people employed by nonprofits</p></div>
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-number">1 in 3</span><p>public service employees work in a nonprofit</p></div>
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-number">~2 in 3</span><p>reporting public charities have revenue under $500,000</p></div>
:::

::: {.lead-in}
Guy & Sowa, Chapter 4; counts from the National Center for Charitable Statistics
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Show of hands: who has worked or volunteered in a nonprofit? Anyone contracted with one?
:::

## Three Failures Theory

::: {.lead-in}
Weisbrod · Hansmann · Salamon
:::

::: {.three-words}
<div class="word-block fragment"><span class="card-heading">Market failure</span><p>No profit in the service, or buyers cannot judge its quality</p></div>
<div class="word-block fragment"><span class="card-heading">Government failure</span><p>Government serves the median voter, so specialized needs go unmet</p></div>
<div class="word-block fragment"><span class="card-heading">Voluntary failure</span><p>Nonprofits lack stable money and reach, so they turn to government as a partner</p></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
The boundaries between sectors are blurry. Government, nonprofits, and businesses often deliver the same public services.
:::

## How Are Nonprofits Different?

::: {.four-corners .roomy-corners}
<div class="corner"><span class="card-heading">Employment at will</span><p>No civil service protections. The employee can be let go for any lawful reason.</p></div>
<div class="corner"><span class="card-heading">No tax base</span><p>Every hire, raise, and benefit needs a funding source.</p></div>
<div class="corner"><span class="card-heading">Flexibility</span><p>No central personnel rules, so the nonprofit designs its own practices. The task is getting the level of structure right.</p></div>
<div class="corner"><span class="card-heading">Specialized missions</span><p>A nonprofit can serve one population. Hiring by protected characteristic is almost never allowed; BFOQs are very narrow and never cover race. Religious organizations may prefer their own members.</p></div>
:::

## Employment At-Will

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">Civil servant</span>

Property interest in the job. Notice, a chance to respond, and an appeal. Merit principles backed by enforceable prohibited practices.

</div>
<div class="compare-side accent"><span class="card-heading">Nonprofit employee</span>

At will unless there is a contract. The law still bars discrimination and many kinds of retaliation. Everything else is up to the organization.

</div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Nonprofits can adopt merit principles on their own, through written policies and an employee handbook.
:::

## Funding and the Starvation Cycle

```{=html}
<div class="cycle" role="img" aria-label="The nonprofit starvation cycle: funders expect low overhead, so the nonprofit underinvests in pay, HR, and training; experienced staff and volunteers leave; service quality and capacity fall; funders then ask for even leaner operations, and the cycle repeats.">
  <div class="cy-box">Funders expect low overhead</div>
  <div class="cy-arrow fragment" data-fragment-index="1">→</div>
  <div class="cy-box fragment" data-fragment-index="1">Underinvest in pay, HR, and training</div>
  <div class="cy-arrow cy-up fragment" data-fragment-index="4">↑<span>…and funders ask for even leaner operations</span></div>
  <div></div>
  <div class="cy-arrow fragment" data-fragment-index="2">↓</div>
  <div class="cy-box fragment" data-fragment-index="3">Service quality and capacity fall</div>
  <div class="cy-arrow fragment" data-fragment-index="3">←</div>
  <div class="cy-box cy-accent fragment" data-fragment-index="2">Experienced staff and volunteers leave</div>
</div>
```

::: {.lead-in}
Gregory & Howard (2009), "The Nonprofit Starvation Cycle"
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Donative labor: the assumption that employees will accept lower pay because they believe in the mission. Mission attachment is not a substitute for competitive pay.
:::

## Managing Volunteers

::: {.pathway .vol-path}
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">Recruit</span><p>Who is in charge of volunteers? A written role description and an application</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">Screen</span><p>Background checks where clients are vulnerable</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">Train</span><p>Orientation, a handbook, and skills for the role</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">Support</span><p>Supervision, logged hours, and feedback</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">Recognize</span><p>Appreciation keeps volunteers coming back</p></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Volunteers need the same basic HR infrastructure as paid staff.
:::

## The Board of Directors

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">What the board does</span>

Hires, evaluates, and if necessary fires the executive director. Keeps the organization on its charitable purpose. Owes duties of care, loyalty, and obedience.

</div>
<div class="compare-side accent"><span class="card-heading">What that means for HR</span>

The executive director reports to the board. The board is responsible for evaluating the executive director and making sure HR policies are in place.

</div>
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Where you work or volunteer: who evaluates the person at the top, and how often?
:::
